blocks.text: Ἡ σύντονος δ᾽ οὖν, καὶ σοφὴ, καὶ τεχνικὴ, [Hē syntonos d' oun, kai sophē, kai technikē,]
She, then, energetic, and wise, and skilled in craft. And in chapter 28,
Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον, [Kai zē men hagnon hē sophē schedon bion,]
And the wise one is wont to live a pure life. Pisides, De mundi opificio, verse 137:

Τίς τὴν μέλιτταν τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν [col. 516] Γεωμετρεῖν ἔπεισε, καὶ τριωρόφους Οἴκους ἐγείρειν ἑξαγώνων κτισμάτων; [Tis tēn melittan tēn sophēn tēn ergatin geōmetrein epeise, kai triōrophous oikous egeirein hexagōnōn ktismatōn?]
Who induced the wise, craftsmanlike bee to practise geometry, and to raise houses of three storeys in hexagonal construction? And further on,
Μή που σε κέντρον τῆς σοφῆς διδασκάλου Πλήξῃ μελίττης, καὶ μαθεῖν ἀναγκάσῃ· [Mē pou se kentron tēs sophēs didaskalou plēxē melittēs, kai mathein anankasē;]

Lest the sting of the bee, that wise teacher, strike you and compel you to learn. Didymus, in book 15 of the Geoponica: Ἡ μέλιττα πάντων τῶν λοιπῶν ζώων ἐστὶ σοφωτάτη, καὶ εὐμηχανωτάτη, καὶ σύνεγγυς ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ τὸ συνετόν [Hē melitta pantōn tōn loipōn zōōn esti sophōtatē, kai eumēchanōtatē, kai synengys anthrōpō kata to syneton]: The bee is the wisest and most ingenious of all animals, and comes closest to the shrewdness of man. Finally the Poet, magnifying the matter in poetic fashion, held that bees have a share of the divine mind. His words are:
Following these signs and these examples, some have said that bees have a share of the divine mind and draughts of the ether. — — — —

The third passage on the honey-making of bees is taken from a book which neither survives in Hebrew nor is acknowledged as canonical by the Hebrews. The Greek words of Ecclesiasticus XI, 3. run thus: Μικρὰ ἐν πετεινοῖς μέλισσα, καὶ ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς· [Mikra en peteinois melissa, kai archē glykasmatōn ho karpos autēs;] The bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. Small among flying creatures: that is, one of the smallest, not absolutely the smallest of flying creatures, as Drusius has it here. For the fly and the gnat are smaller than the bee. Thus Bethlehem was small among the thousands of Judah, yet not the least of all, Matth. II, 6. The beginning of sweet things: that is, supremely sweet, holding first place among sweet things. As in Amos VI, 6. ראשית שמנים, they anoint themselves with the beginning of ointments, that is, with the chief ointment. For the fruit of the bee, which is honey, holds first place among sweet things. Hence the Hebrew proverb, Sweet as honey, of which below. This verse about the bee must be joined with the one immediately preceding: Μὴ αἰνέσῃς ἄνδρα ἐν κάλλει αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ βδελύξῃ ἄνθρωπον ἐν ὁράσει αὐτοῦ [Mē ainesēs andra en kallei autou, kai mē bdelyxē anthrōpon en horasei autou]. Do not praise a man for his beauty [III, 373], nor disdain a man because of his appearance. By these words he does not mean that a man gains no recommendation from his looks; for
Virtue is more pleasing when it comes from a handsome body:

He means only that a man's praise does not chiefly lie in his being outstanding in form, since true praise consists not so much in goods of the body as in goods of the mind. Accordingly, no one is to be despised for his outward appearance, say, if he is rather ugly or short of stature. For often
Greater virtue has reigned in a slight body.

This is proved by the example of the bee, which, however small, yet produces a fruit of remarkable sweetness. Although this is the true meaning of the author, nevertheless Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, chapter 21, understood the same passage quite differently, as his words show: It is said by the wise man: the bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. So too the works of God are ἀνεξιχνίαστα ἐν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, καὶ γλυκύτερα ὑπὲρ μέλι [anexichniasta en anthrōpois, kai thaumasta en hypsēlois, kai glykytera hyper meli], inscrutable among men, and wonderful in the heights, and sweeter than honey. This is partly drawn from verse 5 of the same Sirach: Ὅτι θαυμαστὰ τὰ ἔργα Κυρίου, καὶ κρυπτὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις· [Hoti thaumasta ta erga Kyriou, kai krypta ta erga autou en anthrōpois;] as if that fifth verse were connected with the third, which is about the bee. But it is connected with the fourth, immediately preceding, in which he had told man not to boast, and that there is no reason for him to exalt himself when he is honoured by others. For God, whose works (that is, judgements) are wonderful and inscrutable, can in a single moment cast the proud down from their station and drive them to ruin, as befell Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. IV, 31. and Herod, Act. XII, 23. That this is the true sense of the passage is confirmed by what follows in verses 6 and 7 about tyrants brought down to the ground, the mighty covered with disgrace, and the illustrious delivered into the hands of others.
